pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Grandma Tries a Smart Speaker”, page 1. Scene based on: In the cozy living room of a small family home in Medellín, an elderly grandmother with gray hair and glasses holds a small round smart speaker with a blue light ring, looking confused, while Mateo, 11, and his sister Sara, 11, sit next to her on the sofa. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Grandma Rosa lives with Mateo and Sara.
She wakes up at five every morning.
She drinks coffee and likes to listen to the radio.
Last week, Uncle Pablo gave her a new device.
It’s a small smart speaker with a blue light.
“It plays music and answers questions,” Uncle Pablo says.
Grandma is excited, but she is a little nervous.
On Sunday, she tries to use it.
“Good afternoon, little machine,” she says politely.
“Please play the old songs from my town.”
The speaker doesn’t answer.
The blue light turns on and off.
Grandma looks at Mateo. “Is it sleeping?” she asks.

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Grandma Tries a Smart Speaker”, page 2. Scene based on: The grandmother speaks close to the smart speaker with a long sentence, frustrated, while the speaker's blue light blinks; Mateo laughs a little and Sara covers her mouth, then looks curious. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Grandma tries again with a long sentence.
“Excuse me, can you please play some nice music for me?”
The speaker plays a strange song with loud drums.
Grandma covers her ears. “No, no, no!”
Mateo laughs a little.
“Grandma, the speaker doesn’t understand you,” he says.
“Maybe it’s broken,” Grandma says, frustrated.
“Maybe it doesn’t like old people,” she jokes sadly.
Sara looks at the box of the speaker.
“Wait. Does it speak Spanish?” she asks.
Nobody knows the answer.
Mateo looks for the box under the sofa.

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Grandma Tries a Smart Speaker”, page 3. Scene based on: Sara holds a phone showing the speaker app with only a globe icon and a flag-like color block, pointing at it, while Mateo reads the speaker's small instruction booklet with only pictures, and Grandma watches hopefully. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Sara opens the speaker app on Uncle Pablo’s phone.
She checks the settings.
“The language is English!” she says.
“That’s why it doesn’t understand Grandma.”
Mateo reads the small instruction booklet.
“It understands short commands,” he says.
“It doesn’t understand long, polite sentences.”
Sara changes the language to Spanish.
Then Mateo writes a list of short commands.
“Play music.” “What’s the weather?” “Set a timer.”
Grandma reads the list with her glasses on.
“Only three words? That is easy!” she says.

pages.artDirection: Soft pastel 3D educational storybook, cute rounded characters, bright natural daylight, 11-year-old student context, short concrete A1 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Grandma Tries a Smart Speaker”, page 4. Scene based on: In the morning kitchen, the grandmother smiles and speaks to the smart speaker on the counter while cooking arepas on a griddle, the speaker's blue light glowing, and Mateo and Sara eat breakfast at the table. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Mateo teaches Grandma one command at a time.
“Speak clearly, but not too loud,” he says.
“And use short sentences.”
Grandma practices every afternoon.
Now she uses the speaker every morning.
She asks about the weather before she goes out.
She plays old songs from her town while she cooks.
She uses a timer for the arepas on the stove.
“Ten minutes,” she says, and the speaker counts.
Grandma is proud. “The machine and I are friends now.”
Now Grandma teaches her friends to use it too.
Every Sunday, she shows them a new command.

vocabulary.definition: a small machine with a special use (dispositivo)
a machine that plays sound and music (parlante)
the words people use to communicate, like English (idioma)
a short order you give to a machine (comando)
to pay attention to sounds or words (escuchar)
with a strong sound (fuerte, alto)
songs and sounds people enjoy (música)
the first part of the day (mañana)
a device that counts time (temporizador)
the condition of the air: sun, rain, wind (clima)

quiz.question: Why doesn’t the smart speaker understand Grandma at first?
options: Uncle Pablo forgot to connect it to the internet.
The speaker is broken and needs a new battery.
The speaker’s language is set to English.
Grandma speaks too quietly for the speaker.
quiz.answer: The speaker’s language is set to English.

quiz.question: What happens AFTER Sara changes the language to Spanish?
options: Uncle Pablo gives Grandma the new device.
The speaker plays a strange song with loud drums.
Grandma says, “Good afternoon, little machine,” very politely.
Mateo writes a list of short commands for Grandma.
quiz.answer: Mateo writes a list of short commands for Grandma.

quiz.question: Read: “Mateo teaches Grandma one command at a time.” A “command” is…
options: a short order you give to a machine
a small book with pictures and instructions
a long and polite sentence
a song from an old town
quiz.answer: a short order you give to a machine

quiz.question: What is the story mainly about?
options: An uncle fixes a broken speaker for his whole family.
Two children help their grandmother learn to use a new device.
Two children learn to cook arepas with a timer in the kitchen.
A grandmother buys a new radio for her kitchen.
quiz.answer: Two children help their grandmother learn to use a new device.

quiz.question: Why does Grandma say, “The machine and I are friends now”?
options: The speaker cooks the arepas for her.
She gives the speaker a funny name and a birthday party.
She can use the speaker every day without problems.
The speaker tells her funny jokes every morning.
quiz.answer: She can use the speaker every day without problems.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Plan That Changed at 6:00”, page 1. Scene based on: In the living room of a family home in Medellín on a Saturday afternoon, Valeria, 12, excitedly shows her family a phone screen with only an icon of a fish and a building, while Samuel, 12, her neighbor, sits with them holding a backpack. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: It’s Saturday, and Valeria’s family has a special plan.
They’re going to visit Parque Explora this weekend.
It’s a big science museum in Medellín.
The best part is the aquarium, with fish from the Amazon.
Valeria’s neighbor Samuel is going to come too.
“We’re going to leave at 5:15,” her father says.
“The museum is open until seven today.”
Valeria is very excited.
She’s going to see the big river fish.
It’s her first time at the aquarium.
At 5:15, everybody is ready at the door.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Plan That Changed at 6:00”, page 2. Scene based on: Inside a Medellín Metro train, Valeria looks shocked at her phone showing an icon of a closed door with a clock at six, while her parents frown and Samuel leans over to read the screen. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On the Metro, Valeria’s phone buzzes.
It’s an announcement from the museum.
“Today the museum is going to close early, at six.”
“We’re sorry for the inconvenience.”
Valeria looks at the time. It’s 5:40.
“We’re going to have only twenty minutes!” she says.
Her father sighs. “Then we aren’t going to go.”
“We’re going to go home,” her mother says.
Valeria feels very disappointed.
She was waiting for this all week.
Samuel reads the message again, slowly.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Plan That Changed at 6:00”, page 3. Scene based on: Samuel points at a small line at the bottom of the phone message showing an icon of a dome with stars and a clock at eight, while Valeria wipes her eyes and looks at the screen with new hope. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: “Wait. Look at the last line,” Samuel says.
“The planetarium next door isn’t closing early.”
“It’s open until eight tonight.”
“There’s a show about the stars at 6:30.”
Valeria stops being sad for a moment.
“The planetarium is only five minutes away,” she says.
“What are we going to do if we go there?”
Her father thinks about it.
“We’re going to see the stars,” he says.
“Not the fish, but the stars.”
“And we’re going to visit the aquarium next Saturday.”

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Plan That Changed at 6:00”, page 4. Scene based on: Outside the planetarium in Medellín at dusk, Valeria's family and Samuel walk toward a large white dome building with lights turning on, Valeria carrying a printed ticket and Samuel pointing at the sky where the first stars appear. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Everybody likes Samuel’s suggestion.
They get off the Metro at the Universidad station.
The museum is closing, and many people are leaving.
But the planetarium is open and full of light.
Valeria’s father buys four tickets for the show.
“We’re going to sit in the middle,” Valeria says.
“From there, we’re going to see the whole dome.”
Samuel looks at the evening sky outside.
The first stars are appearing over the hills.
“Real stars before the show!” he laughs.

pages.artDirection: Painterly digital educational illustration, soft brushwork, gentle outlines, vivid but soft colors, 12-year-old student context, clear A1+ English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Plan That Changed at 6:00”, page 5. Scene based on: Inside the dark planetarium dome, Valeria and Samuel lean back in reclined seats looking up at a projection of the Milky Way and planets, their faces lit by soft blue light, Valeria's parents smiling next to them. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: The show is amazing.
The dome becomes a sky full of stars and planets.
Valeria sees Saturn’s rings and Jupiter’s big red spot.
“I’m going to be an astronomer,” she whispers.
After the show, they walk to the Metro.
“Are you still disappointed?” Samuel asks.
“No,” Valeria says. “The plan changed, but it was great.”
“If we didn’t read the message, we were going home.”
Her father laughs. “Next Saturday, the fish. Promise.”
That night, Valeria writes her new plan in her diary.
“Next Saturday: aquarium. Then planetarium again!”

vocabulary.definition: a list of things you are going to do (plan)
Saturday and Sunday (fin de semana)
the time between afternoon and night (atardecer)
a building where you can see interesting objects (museo)
a place where you can see fish and sea animals (acuario)
important information said to the public (anuncio)
to stop being open (cerrar)
an idea for others to consider (sugerencia)
a place with a dome that shows the stars (planetario)
sad because something did not happen (decepcionado)

quiz.question: What time does the museum close on Saturday?
options: At eight o’clock
At seven o’clock
At six o’clock
quiz.answer: At six o’clock

quiz.question: What happens because Samuel reads the last line of the message?
options: The family goes to the planetarium show instead of going home.
The family arrives at the aquarium just before it closes at six.
Valeria’s father buys tickets for next Saturday.
The museum decides to stay open until seven.
quiz.answer: The family goes to the planetarium show instead of going home.

quiz.question: What is the main idea of the story?
options: Museums in Medellín always close early on Saturdays.
When a plan changes, careful reading can lead to a good new plan.
Families should never use the Metro on weekends because it’s full.
Planetariums are more interesting than aquariums.
quiz.answer: When a plan changes, careful reading can lead to a good new plan.

quiz.question: Why does Valeria feel disappointed on the Metro?
options: Her father forgot to buy the tickets for the aquarium show.
The Metro is too slow to arrive at the museum before it closes.
She was excited about the aquarium, and now there isn’t enough time.
Samuel doesn’t want to go to the museum with her family.
quiz.answer: She was excited about the aquarium, and now there isn’t enough time.

quiz.question: Read: “Everybody likes Samuel’s suggestion.” A “suggestion” is…
options: a dome that shows the stars
important information for the public
a building with interesting objects
an idea for others to consider
quiz.answer: an idea for others to consider

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 1. Scene based on: In a small family apartment in Medellín at 5:59 pm, Camila, 13, sits on the sofa staring at a phone showing a bright message bubble with a robot icon and a big clock icon, her finger ready to tap, while Mateo, 13, beside her looks at the screen with a frown. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: It’s Friday afternoon, and Camila is relaxing at home.
Her friend Mateo is studying with her.
At 5:59, her phone shows a new message.
It’s an invitation to a youth robotics camp.
“Last chance! Registration closes at 6:00!” it says.
“Click the link now and reserve your place!”
Camila loves robots. This is her dream.
She is moving her finger to the link.
“Only one minute! I’m registering right now!” she says.
Mateo puts his hand on her phone.
“Wait. Something looks strange,” he says.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 2. Scene based on: Camila looks frustrated at Mateo, pulling her phone back, while Mateo points at the screen where the web address appears as a strange jumble of random symbols and a warning triangle icon. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Camila is frustrated. “We’re losing time!”
“The deadline is in one minute!” she says.
Mateo points at the web address in the message.
It has strange letters and numbers.
It isn’t the city’s youth website.
“Who is sending this message?” he asks.
Camila looks again. It’s from an unknown number.
“And look. It’s asking for your ID number.”
“It’s also asking for your parents’ bank card.”
Camila stops. That is very suspicious.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 3. Scene based on: Camila and Mateo sit at a desk looking at a laptop showing a clean government-style youth website with only icons of a robot, a calendar and a shield, comparing it with the suspicious phone message lying beside the laptop. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: “Let’s find the official information,” Mateo says.
They open the laptop and search for the city’s youth institute.
They find the real website easily.
There is a page about the robotics camp.
The camp is real, and it’s free for students.
But the registration isn’t closing today.
“Registration is closing next Friday,” Camila reads.
“Parents are registering their children online or in person.”
“The institute never asks for bank cards.”
Camila’s face turns red.

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 4. Scene based on: Camila holds her phone and shows a screenshot of the scam message to her mother, a woman in her forties with reading glasses, in the living room, while Mateo stands beside them looking serious. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Camila understands now.
The first message was a scam.
“They wanted my personal data and money,” she says.
“And they used my favorite thing: robots.”
Mateo nods. “They are using the clock to make you hurry.”
“When you hurry, you don’t think.”
Camila’s mother comes home at 6:30.
Camila shows her the message and the real website.
“You did the right thing,” her mother says.
“We’re registering together on Monday, after work.”

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 5. Scene based on: On Monday evening at the dining table, Camila and her mother register on the official youth website on a laptop showing only a robot icon and a green check mark, while Mateo shows a thumbs up on a video call. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Monday, Camila and her mother register on the official website.
They’re filling the form together, step by step.
The form doesn’t ask for bank cards or passwords.
It asks for the school name and a parent’s phone.
At the end, a green message appears.
“Your registration is confirmed. The camp is starting July 10.”
Camila jumps and hugs her mother.
“I’m going to the robotics camp!” she shouts.
She sends Mateo a message with a robot sticker.
“Thanks for stopping my finger on Friday!”

pages.artDirection: Vivid 3D educational storybook illustration, warm light, dynamic teenage poses, 13-year-old student context, accessible A2 English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Invitation at 5:59”, page 6. Scene based on: In the school hallway, Camila stands next to a small handmade poster with only icons of a clock, a warning triangle, a shield and a check mark, explaining it to a group of interested classmates while Mateo helps hold the poster. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Wednesday, Camila tells her class about the scam.
Some classmates received the same message.
Two of them almost clicked the link too.
Camila and Mateo are making a poster for the school.
It has four simple tips.
“If a message is rushing you, stop.”
“Check who is sending it.”
“Find the official website yourself.”
“Never share bank cards or passwords.”
The teacher hangs the poster next to the classroom door.

vocabulary.definition: a message that asks you to join an event (invitación)
words or a button that opens a web page (enlace)
the act of signing up for an event (inscripción)
the time when something must be finished (fecha límite)
making you think something is wrong (sospechoso)
from a real government or organization (oficial)
a group of pages on the internet (sitio web)
private information about a person (datos personales)
a dishonest trick to get money or information (estafa)
an event where young people learn and do activities (campamento)

quiz.question: When does the real registration for the robotics camp close?
options: Next Friday
On Monday after work
At 6:00 on Friday
On July 10
quiz.answer: Next Friday

quiz.question: Why does Mateo stop Camila from clicking the link?
options: The link opens the official website of the city.
The message looks suspicious and comes from an unknown number.
He wants to register for the robotics camp before her.
He doesn’t want Camila to go to the robotics camp in July.
quiz.answer: The message looks suspicious and comes from an unknown number.

quiz.question: Why does the author mention that the message uses a one-minute deadline?
options: To explain how the city’s official youth website works.
To show that robotics camps are very popular.
To show how scams make people hurry so they don’t think.
To show that Camila is always late.
quiz.answer: To show how scams make people hurry so they don’t think.

quiz.question: What is the main idea of the story?
options: Robotics camps are only for students who register very fast.
Students should never use their phones on Fridays.
Parents should register their children for every camp.
Checking official sources protects you from online scams.
quiz.answer: Checking official sources protects you from online scams.

quiz.question: Read: “That is very suspicious.” “Suspicious” means…
options: making you think something is wrong
confirmed and finished
very exciting, new, and fun to see
official and safe
quiz.answer: making you think something is wrong

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 1. Scene based on: In a Medellín public school classroom set up for a debate, Santiago, 14, stands confidently pointing at a screen with a picture of a humanoid robot and a red X over workers, while Laura, 14, sits with her arms crossed and a skeptical look. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Santiago’s class is having a debate on Friday.
The teacher shows a photo of a robot in a factory.
The topic is “Will robots take our jobs?”
Santiago is very sure about his opinion.
“Robots will take every job in Medellín,” he says.
“Factories, stores, buses, everything.”
“There won’t be any jobs for us in the future.”
Some classmates look worried.
Laura raises her hand.
“Do you have evidence, or is that only a feeling?”
Santiago doesn’t answer immediately.
“Everyone knows it,” he says finally.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 2. Scene based on: Santiago and Laura sit at a library table with a notebook showing a list of jobs as small icons: a shopping cart, a bus, a nurse's cross, scissors and a factory gear, both thinking hard. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: After class, Laura has an idea.
“Let’s investigate real jobs in our neighborhood,” she says.
“Then we can use facts in the debate.”
Santiago agrees, but he still thinks he’s right.
They choose five jobs to study.
A supermarket cashier, a bus driver, and a nurse.
A hairdresser and a textile factory worker.
“We’ll interview people this weekend,” Laura says.
“We’ll ask what machines already do in their jobs.”
Santiago writes the questions in his notebook.
He doesn’t believe the answers will change his mind.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 3. Scene based on: In a Medellín supermarket, a friendly middle-aged cashier talks to Santiago and Laura near a row of self-checkout machines, while customers scan their own products in the background. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: First, they visit a supermarket near school.
They talk to Doña Ruth, a cashier for fifteen years.
“Last year, the store installed self-checkout machines,” she says.
“Now there are fewer cashiers in the afternoon.”
Santiago looks at Laura. “See? Robots!”
“But I wasn’t fired,” Doña Ruth continues.
“Now I help customers with the machines.”
“I also organize the products and solve problems.”
“Some tasks changed, but people are still needed.”
Laura writes, “Jobs may change, not only disappear.”
Santiago doesn’t say anything. He is thinking.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 4. Scene based on: Inside a large textile factory in the Medellín area, a factory worker in her thirties monitors an automated weaving machine on a tablet screen showing only graphs and icons, while Santiago and Laura watch with visitor vests. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Next, they visit Laura’s aunt at a textile factory.
“Twenty years ago, cutting fabric was done by hand,” she says.
“Now a computer machine does that task.”
“Many cutting jobs disappeared,” she admits.
“But I learned to control the machines.”
“Now I need computer skills, not only sewing skills.”
Santiago is quiet. This is real automation.
“So some jobs might disappear,” he says.
“Yes. That’s true,” Laura says.
“But new jobs might appear too.”

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 5. Scene based on: A nurse in a white uniform in a health clinic hallway holds the hand of an elderly patient while talking to Santiago and Laura, and a hairdresser cuts a child's hair in a small salon next door, both scenes visible in one wide street view. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They also talk to a nurse and a hairdresser.
“A machine may measure blood pressure,” the nurse says.
“But it can’t calm a scared patient.”
The hairdresser laughs at the robot question.
“A robot might cut hair one day,” she says.
“But my clients come to talk, too.”
“They might not want to talk to a machine.”
Santiago and Laura compare all their notes.
Jobs with simple, repeated tasks may be automated.
Jobs with care, creativity, and conversation might change less.
“Robots might replace some tasks, not all people,” Laura says.

pages.artDirection: Semi-realistic painted educational cartoon, rich natural light, detailed props, cinematic framing, 14-year-old student context, A2+ connected English. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “Will Robots Take This Job?”, page 6. Scene based on: On debate day in the classroom, Santiago and Laura stand together at the front presenting a chart with icons of jobs in three colors, while classmates listen with interest and the teacher takes notes. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Friday, the debate begins.
Santiago stands up to speak first.
“Last week, I said robots will take every job.”
“Now I have evidence, and my opinion is different.”
“Some jobs may disappear, like some cutting jobs.”
“Other jobs might change, like cashiers’ jobs.”
“And new jobs may appear, like machine technicians.”
Laura adds the most important idea.
“The best protection is learning new skills.”
The teacher smiles. “That’s a strong, honest argument.”
“Changing your opinion with evidence is a skill too.”
Santiago laughs. “Then I learned two skills this week.”

vocabulary.definition: a machine that can do tasks automatically (robot)
the use of machines to do work people did before (automatización)
a piece of work you have to do (tarea)
equipment that uses power to do work (máquina)
to take the place of something or someone (reemplazar)
a person who takes money in a store (cajero)
an ability you develop with practice (habilidad)
a formal discussion with different opinions (debate)
facts that show something is true (evidencia)
the time that will come after now (futuro)

quiz.question: What happened at Doña Ruth’s supermarket last year?
options: The store hired more cashiers for the afternoon.
The store installed self-checkout machines.
The store replaced all the products with robots.
The store closed and all cashiers lost their jobs.
quiz.answer: The store installed self-checkout machines.

quiz.question: Why does Laura ask Santiago if he has evidence?
options: She knows that robots will take every job in Medellín very soon.
She wants to win the debate by making Santiago angry.
She thinks his strong opinion is based only on a feeling.
She thinks Santiago should not speak in class.
quiz.answer: She thinks his strong opinion is based only on a feeling.

quiz.question: How are the textile factory worker’s experience and Doña Ruth’s experience similar?
options: Both of them lost their jobs because of robots last year.
Both of them say that machines are useless and break all the time.
Both of them work in the same supermarket near the school.
Both of them still work, but their tasks changed because of machines.
quiz.answer: Both of them still work, but their tasks changed because of machines.

quiz.question: What is the main message of the text?
options: Automation may change many jobs, so learning new skills is important.
Robots will take every job in Medellín very soon.
Students should not talk about robots and the future during class.
Nurses and hairdressers will soon be replaced by machines.
quiz.answer: Automation may change many jobs, so learning new skills is important.

quiz.question: Read: “This is real automation.” “Automation” means…
options: a formal discussion with very different opinions
the use of machines to do work people did before
a person who takes money in a store
facts that show something is true
quiz.answer: the use of machines to do work people did before

10.label: 10° Grade / B1 Beginner
10.title: The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 1. Scene based on: In the lobby of a public library in Medellín, Valentina, 16, wearing a volunteer badge, holds a clipboard with a schedule while people arrive for a youth forum; Mateo, 16, carries a box of name tags, and a clock on the wall shows 3:50. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Saturday, Valentina is organizing a youth forum on climate.
It’s starting at four in the library auditorium.
One hundred students are coming from different schools.
The main speaker is an environmental engineer.
She is giving a talk about water in Medellín.
Valentina is a volunteer organizer with her friend Mateo.
At 3:50, everything looks perfect.
The chairs are ready, and the microphones are working.
Then Valentina’s phone rings.
It’s the speaker, and she sounds stressed.
“I’m stuck in traffic. There’s an accident on the highway.”

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 2. Scene based on: Inside the library auditorium, water drips from the ceiling onto the front rows of chairs and a small puddle forms near the stage, while a library worker places a bucket and Valentina stands frozen holding her phone. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: “I’ll arrive at 4:30, maybe later,” the speaker says.
Valentina’s heart starts beating fast.
Then a library worker runs out of the auditorium.
“There’s a leak in the ceiling!” he says.
“The rain is coming through above the stage.”
Water is falling on the first rows of chairs.
Students are arriving, and the hall is getting noisy.
Valentina looks at the clock. It’s 3:52.
“We’ll have to cancel everything,” she says.
She feels like crying.
“No speaker and no auditorium. It’s a disaster.”

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 3. Scene based on: Mateo calmly holds up three fingers while talking to Valentina in the busy library lobby, a notebook in his other hand with three simple icons: a clock, a door and a microphone. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Mateo puts down the box of name tags.
“Wait. Let’s separate facts from fears,” he says.
“Fact one: the speaker will arrive, but she’ll be late.”
“Fact two: the auditorium has a leak.”
“Fact three: one hundred students are here now.”
“The forum isn’t cancelled. It’s only changing.”
Valentina takes a deep breath.
“Okay. Is there another room in the library?” she asks.
Mateo asks the librarian at the front desk.
“Room 2 is free until seven,” she says.
“It has sixty chairs and a projector.”

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 4. Scene based on: Valentina speaks into a microphone in the library lobby to a crowd of arriving students, pointing toward a hallway, while Mateo and two volunteers carry extra chairs into a smaller room. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Valentina takes a microphone in the lobby.
“Good afternoon, everybody!” she says.
“I have two small changes to announce.”
“First, we’re moving to Room 2 because of a leak.”
“Second, our speaker has a short delay.”
“So we’re starting with a student panel at four.”
Some students look surprised, but nobody complains.
Mateo and other volunteers carry forty extra chairs.
Room 2 is small, but it’s dry and bright.
At 4:05, everybody is sitting and ready.
Some students are even sitting on the floor, happily.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 5. Scene based on: In a smaller bright library room, four teenage students sit at a table in front of a full audience speaking about climate projects, one holding a small plant, another showing a water bottle, while Valentina moderates with a microphone. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Valentina invites four students to the front.
They’re forming a panel about local climate projects.
One student talks about a school garden.
Another talks about saving water at home.
A third explains a project to clean a creek.
The audience asks many questions.
Nobody is thinking about the missing speaker now.
“This is better than I expected,” Valentina whispers.
Mateo smiles. “Students like hearing other students.”
The audience laughs at a funny story about a creek.
At 4:35, the door opens quietly.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 6. Scene based on: The environmental engineer, a woman in her forties with a backpack and a laptop, enters the small room smiling and is welcomed by applause, while Valentina gives her the microphone and the student panel makes space at the table. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: The engineer enters the room, a little wet from the rain.
Everybody claps for her.
“I’m so sorry for the delay,” she says.
“But I heard your panel from the hallway. Wonderful!”
She connects her laptop and starts her talk.
She connects her ideas to the students’ projects.
“You’re already doing what I’ll explain today,” she says.
The forum ends at six, thirty minutes late.
But nobody leaves early.
Many students stay to talk with the engineer.
Some of them take photos with her.

pages.artDirection: Modern semi-realistic cinematic educational illustration, natural urban light, 15–16-year-old student context, B1 English with clear reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Event That Changed in Ten Minutes”, page 7. Scene based on: After the forum, Valentina and Mateo sit on the library steps in the evening rain under a roof, tired but smiling, Valentina writing in a notebook with a simple drawing of a backup plan with arrows. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: After the forum, Valentina and Mateo sit on the steps outside.
“Ten minutes before four, I wanted to cancel,” Valentina admits.
“Ten minutes is enough to change a plan,” Mateo says.
“Not enough to panic, but enough to think.”
Valentina writes a note for the next forum.
“We’ll always have a backup room.”
“We’ll prepare a student activity in case of a delay.”
“And we’ll check the auditorium roof when it’s rainy.”
She closes the notebook and looks at the rain.
Mateo laughs. “That last one is very specific.”
“Yes, but now it’s on my list,” Valentina says.

vocabulary.definition: a meeting where people discuss a topic (foro)
a person who gives a talk to a group (conferencista)
a large room for talks and shows (auditorio)
water that comes through a hole by accident (gotera)
time when something is later than expected (retraso)
the people who watch or listen to an event (público)
to tell people something officially (anunciar)
a small group of people who discuss a topic in public (panel)
a device that makes your voice louder (micrófono)
a person who helps without being paid (voluntario)

quiz.question: Why is the speaker late?
options: She forgot the time of the forum.
She is preparing her talk in another room of the library.
She is stuck in traffic because of an accident on the highway.
She is waiting for the heavy rain to stop before she leaves home.
quiz.answer: She is stuck in traffic because of an accident on the highway.

quiz.question: Why does Mateo say, “Let’s separate facts from fears”?
options: He wants to go home because of the rain.
He believes the auditorium is not really wet.
He thinks the speaker is lying about the traffic on the highway.
He wants Valentina to see the forum can change, not end.
quiz.answer: He wants Valentina to see the forum can change, not end.

quiz.question: Why does the author include the student panel?
options: To show how a quick new activity can keep the audience involved.
To show that the engineer was not needed at the forum at all.
To describe the history of the library.
To explain why students don’t like long talks.
quiz.answer: To show how a quick new activity can keep the audience involved.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between the leak and Room 2?
options: Room 2 is bigger, so they choose it from the beginning of the day.
The leak in the auditorium makes the group move to Room 2.
The leak is in Room 2, so they cancel the forum.
Room 2 has a leak, so they stay in the auditorium.
quiz.answer: The leak in the auditorium makes the group move to Room 2.

quiz.question: Which statement best summarizes the text?
options: Forums should always be cancelled when speakers are late.
Libraries in Medellín have many problems with leaks when it rains.
Calm thinking can turn last-minute problems into a successful event.
Student panels are always more important than expert speakers.
quiz.answer: Calm thinking can turn last-minute problems into a successful event.

11.label: 11° Grade / B1+
11.title: The Product That Crossed Three Countries

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 1. Scene based on: In a small family apartment in the Manrique neighborhood of Medellín, Sofía, 17, holds a fancy imported chocolate bar box and reads the small label on the back with a frown, while Mateo, 17, looks over her shoulder holding a cup of hot chocolate. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Sofía’s aunt sends her a gift from a department store.
It’s an expensive box of Swiss chocolate.
Sofía reads the label on the back of the box.
“Cacao from Colombia,” it says in small letters.
“Made in Switzerland. Packed in Germany.”
Sofía laughs. “This chocolate crossed three countries!”
“And it started here, in Colombia.”
Her friend Mateo is visiting to study.
“So Colombian chocolate traveled to Europe and back?” he asks.
“Why didn’t they just make it here?”
Sofía doesn’t know. She decides to find out.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 2. Scene based on: On a cacao farm in the green hills of Antioquia, a smiling farmer in his fifties with a straw hat shows Sofía and Mateo yellow cacao pods growing on a tree, opening one to reveal white beans. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: For their economics project, they research cacao.
Sofía’s uncle has a small farm in Antioquia.
On the weekend, they visit him.
Cacao pods are growing on the trees, yellow and orange.
“We harvest the pods by hand,” the farmer says.
“Then the beans are fermented and dried in the sun.”
“Most of our dry beans are sold to big companies.”
“Some of them are exported to Europe.”
“Do you get a good price?” Mateo asks.
The uncle shrugs. “Not as good as we want.”
“Prices change every year, and we can’t control them.”

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 3. Scene based on: On a laptop at a kitchen table, Sofía and Mateo look at a simple map with arrows from Colombia to Switzerland and Germany and back to Colombia, with icons of cacao beans, a factory and a ship, while Mateo calculates on paper. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Back in Medellín, they follow the chocolate’s journey.
First, the cacao was grown and harvested in Colombia.
Then the dry beans were shipped to Europe.
Companies export tons of beans every year.
In Switzerland, the beans were roasted and ground.
The chocolate was mixed, molded, and wrapped.
Then the bars were packed in boxes in Germany.
Finally, the boxes were shipped back to Colombia.
“It traveled about twenty thousand kilometers,” Mateo calculates.
“Just to return to the country where it started.”
Sofía shakes her head in surprise.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 4. Scene based on: Sofía and Mateo compare two price tags on a table drawn only as coin icons: a small pile of coins next to a pile of raw cacao beans and a very large pile of coins next to the shiny imported chocolate box. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Then they compare prices.
A farmer receives little money for one kilo of beans.
But the Swiss chocolate costs many times more per kilo.
“Where does all that money go?” Sofía asks.
They read reports and economic articles.
Companies process the beans in their own countries.
Most of the money stays there.
Roasting, mixing, branding, and marketing add value.
“The richest steps happened far from the farm,” Mateo says.
“The farmers only sell the raw material.”
Sofía writes, “Value is added after the harvest.”

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 5. Scene based on: At the port of Cartagena, large shipping containers are inspected by customs officers in uniforms with tablets, while Sofía and Mateo watch a short documentary scene on a laptop showing only icons of a ship, a box and a stamp. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They also learn about customs.
Imported products are checked when they arrive.
Taxes are paid, and documents are reviewed.
The Swiss chocolate was taxed when it entered Colombia.
“So we import our own cacao as chocolate,” Sofía says.
“And we pay more for it.”
Mateo finds another surprising fact.
Some Colombian cacao is considered among the best in the world.
It’s often called “fine flavor” cacao.
“So the best part was already ours,” Sofía says.
Mateo nods. “We exported our best part.”

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 6. Scene based on: In a small chocolate workshop in Medellín, a young woman chocolate maker in an apron shows Sofía and Mateo shiny chocolate bars being made, with cacao beans in sacks and a roasting machine behind her. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: Mateo finds a small chocolate company in Medellín.
On Saturday, they visit its workshop.
The owner, Daniela, is twenty-nine years old.
“Our cacao is bought directly from farmers,” she says.
“We pay them more than the big companies.”
“Then the chocolate is made here, in Medellín.”
The beans are roasted, ground, and molded in the workshop.
“So the value stays in Colombia,” Sofía says.
“Exactly. And more jobs are created here,” Daniela answers.
She gives them a small bar to taste.
The paper wrapper was designed by a local artist.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 7. Scene based on: Sofía and Mateo sit on a bench outside the workshop tasting dark chocolate and comparing it with the Swiss box, both smiling, the hillsides of Medellín behind them in the late afternoon. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: They taste the local chocolate on a bench outside.
“It’s different,” Mateo says. “Stronger and more fruity.”
“I like it better,” Sofía admits.
“And it didn’t cross three countries.”
She thinks about her uncle on the farm.
“If more chocolate were made here, farmers might earn more.”
Mateo agrees, but he isn’t sure it’s simple.
“Big factories have machines and famous brands,” he says.
“Small companies have to compete with them.”
“That’s true. But consumers can choose,” Sofía answers.
They decide to buy two bars for their families.

pages.artDirection: Realistic cinematic digital educational illustration, mature high-school atmosphere, 17–18-year-old student context, B1+ connected English with nuanced reasoning. One single 4:5 vertical scene for “The Product That Crossed Three Countries”, page 8. Scene based on: In a classroom, Sofía and Mateo present a poster showing the journey of a chocolate bar as arrows across a world map, next to a table with the Swiss chocolate box and a local chocolate bar, while classmates taste small pieces. Natural expressions, age-appropriate, educational, school-safe, no visible text, no letters, no logos.

sentences.html: On Monday, they present their project in class.
They show the map with the chocolate’s long journey.
“This chocolate was grown here and made in Europe,” Sofía says.
“Most of its value was created outside Colombia.”
Then Mateo shares the local chocolate with the class.
“This one was grown and made in our country.”
The students taste both chocolates.
Many prefer the local one, and it’s cheaper.
Some want to visit the workshop with their families.
The teacher asks, “What did you learn about labels?”
“A label tells a story,” Sofía answers.
“But you have to read it carefully.”

vocabulary.definition: the bean used to make chocolate (cacao)
a person who grows crops or raises animals (agricultor)
to collect crops from the fields (cosechar)
to sell products to another country (exportar)
to change a raw material into a product (procesar)
to buy products from another country (importar)
the office that checks products entering a country (aduana)
a small paper with information about a product (etiqueta)
how much something is worth (valor)
from the area where you live (local)

quiz.question: According to the label, where was the chocolate packed?
options: In Switzerland
In Colombia
In Antioquia
In Germany
quiz.answer: In Germany

quiz.question: Why do the farmers receive only a small part of the chocolate’s final price?
options: The most valuable steps happen far from the farm.
The farmers do not harvest the pods themselves.
The cacao from Colombia has the lowest quality in the world.
The farmers sell their cacao only in Medellín.
quiz.answer: The most valuable steps happen far from the farm.

quiz.question: Why does the author include the visit to Daniela’s chocolate workshop?
options: To show that Swiss chocolate is better than local chocolate.
To show an example where cacao’s value stays in Colombia.
To show that local chocolate is always more expensive.
To explain how customs officers check imported products.
quiz.answer: To show an example where cacao’s value stays in Colombia.

quiz.question: Read: “Roasting, mixing, branding, and marketing add value.” Here, “value” means…
options: the label on the back of a box
the office that checks products
how much something is worth
the beans used to make chocolate
quiz.answer: how much something is worth

quiz.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the text?
options: Labels on food products are not important to read.
Colombian farmers should stop growing cacao.
Imported chocolate is always better than local Colombian chocolate.
Where a product is processed affects who earns money from it.
quiz.answer: Where a product is processed affects who earns money from it.
